chapters.title: Object modeling: an elevator system
chapters.tagline: State plus behaviour, objects that own their data, and a brain you can swap
goals: Say what an object is (state + behaviour) and how a class differs from an instance
Build a system by composition: a Building has Floors and Elevators
Explain encapsulation with a bug you can actually trigger (shared state)
Model an elevator as a state machine with four states
Swap scheduling policies (FIFO vs SCAN) with the strategy pattern, and measure the difference

sections.title: An elevator is a bundle of objects

blocks.html:
Press the call button in a lift lobby. Something decides which car comes, which way it goes and when the doors open. That "something" is not one big function. It's a handful of small objects, each responsible for one thing:

  • the Building holds everything together,
  • each Floor knows who is waiting on it,
  • the Elevator knows where it is and what it is doing,
  • a Policy decides where the elevator should go next.

Before any code, play with them. Every block is one object. Click it and it tells you what it is responsible for, and why it owns that piece of data and not some other object.

blocks.name: bx-elevator
blocks.title: Floors, a car, a queue and a policy
blocks.goal: Run the burst of 7 calls with FIFO, then switch to SCAN and serve the same burst. SCAN must beat FIFO.
blocks.intro: Watch the car under FIFO: it drives straight past floor 1 on its way up to 8. Then click the green policy block.

blocks.q: In the simulation, why does the request queue belong to the Building rather than to the Elevator?

opts.t: Because the elevator is too small to hold a list
Because the policy needs to see every call to plan a route, and a call exists before any car is chosen
Because Python lists can't be stored inside objects
It doesn't matter at all where data lives

blocks.why: A call is made to the building: "someone on floor 6 wants a lift". Only later does a policy pick a car. If each car kept its own list, a second car could never help, and the policy couldn't see the whole picture.

sections.title: An object is state plus behaviour

blocks.html:
An object bundles two things:

  • state: the data it remembers (an elevator's current floor),
  • behaviour: the things it can do, written as functions called methods (move_to).

A class is the blueprint. An instance is one real thing made from it. Elevator() builds a new instance; inside methods, self means "the instance this was called on". Two instances made from the same class have their own state: moving one doesn't move the other.

blocks.code:
class Elevator:
    def __init__(self, floor=0):
        self.floor = floor

    def move_to(self, target):
        trip = abs(target - self.floor)
        self.floor = target
        return trip

a = Elevator()
b = Elevator(5)
print(a.move_to(3), a.floor)
print(b.move_to(3), b.floor)
print(a is b, a.floor == b.floor)

blocks.html: Now give the elevator a second piece of state: a running total of floors travelled. The method that moves the car is the only place that should update it, so the number can never drift away from the truth.

blocks.title: travelled_counter
blocks.prompt: Fill the two blanks. __init__ must start the counter at zero, and move_to must add the length of each trip to it before changing the floor.
blocks.tests:
e = Elevator()
assert e.travelled == 0, "a brand-new elevator has travelled 0 floors"
e.move_to(8); e.move_to(1)
assert e.travelled == 15, f"0→8 is 8 floors, 8→1 is 7 more: 15 in total, got {e.travelled}"
assert e.floor == 1, "the car should end on floor 1"
other = Elevator(4)
assert other.travelled == 0, "each instance has its own counter: moving e must not change another elevator"
hints: The counter goes up by trip every time: self.travelled + trip.

sections.title: Composition: a building has floors and elevators

blocks.html:
Real systems are built by putting objects inside other objects. A Building doesn't inherit from Elevator ("a building is a kind of elevator" makes no sense). It has elevators. This is called composition, and it's the main way objects are combined.

Objects then talk by message passing: calling each other's methods. The building doesn't reach in and set car.floor = 3. It sends a message, car.add_stop(3), and the car decides how to get there. The sender only needs to know what to ask, not how the other object works.

blocks.title: A Building that dispatches the nearest car
blocks.tests:
b = Building(6, 2)
b.elevators[1].floor = 5
car = b.call(4)
assert car is b.elevators[1], "the car on floor 5 is nearer to floor 4 than the car on floor 0"
assert car.stops == [4], "the building sends a message: add_stop(4)"
assert car.floor == 5, "the building must not teleport the car; only the car moves itself"
assert b.floors[4].waiting == 1, "floor 4 now has one person waiting"
lines: nearest = min(self.elevators, key=lambda e: abs(e.floor - floor))

sections.title: Encapsulation: every instance owns its own state

blocks.html:
Encapsulation means each object guards its own data, and everyone else goes through its methods. Python doesn't lock anything; the convention is a leading underscore (self._stops) meaning "private: please use my methods".

But there's a sneakier way to break ownership: two objects accidentally sharing the same list. A default argument like stops=[] is created once, when the function is defined, and then reused by every call. Predict what happens.
Two cars, one shared to-do list: press a button for car A and car B also heads there. That's exactly the kind of bug encapsulation is meant to prevent, and it hides in plain sight.

blocks.title: shared_stops
blocks.prompt: Car b keeps receiving car a's stops. Fix __init__ so that every elevator gets its own list, while still allowing Elevator(stops=[2, 5]).
blocks.tests:
a, b = Elevator(), Elevator()
a.add_stop(3)
assert b.stops() == [], f"car b should have no stops, but it sees {b.stops()}: the two cars share one list"
assert a.stops() == [3], "car a should have its own stop"
given = [2, 5]
c = Elevator(stops=given)
c.add_stop(7)
assert c.stops() == [2, 5, 7], "passing stops in should still work"
assert given == [2, 5], "the caller's list must not change: the elevator should copy it"
hints: Use None as the default and create a fresh list inside __init__: [] written there runs on every call.
To protect the caller's list too, store a copy: list(stops).

sections.title: A state machine: four states and clear rules

blocks.html:
What is an elevator doing right now? At any moment it is in exactly one of four states:

StateMeaning
IDLEstopped, doors shut, waiting for work
MOVING_UP / MOVING_DOWNtravelling one floor per tick
DOORS_OPENstopped at a floor, people getting in

Each tick (one second of time), a rule picks the next state from the current state, the floor and the target. Writing the rules as a tiny table, instead of scattering ifs and flags like is_moving and doors_open all over the code, makes impossible combinations (moving with the doors open!) impossible to even represent. This is a state machine.

blocks.title: next_state
blocks.prompt:
Write next_state(state, floor, target). target is the floor to head for, or None if there's no work. Rules, checked in this order:

  1. If the doors are open, they close: the next state is "IDLE".
  2. No target: "IDLE".
  3. Target above: "MOVING_UP". Below: "MOVING_DOWN".
  4. Already at the target: "DOORS_OPEN".
blocks.tests:
assert next_state("IDLE", 0, None) == "IDLE", "no work: stay idle"
assert next_state("IDLE", 0, 5) == "MOVING_UP", "target above: go up"
assert next_state("MOVING_UP", 5, 2) == "MOVING_DOWN", "target below: go down"
assert next_state("MOVING_UP", 5, 5) == "DOORS_OPEN", "arrived: open the doors"
assert next_state("DOORS_OPEN", 5, 7) == "IDLE", "doors must close before the car moves again, even if there's more work"
hints: Check the rules top to bottom with if ... return. The order matters: rule 1 must win even when there is a target.

blocks.html: Here is the whole elevator ticking with those rules. Read the trace: notice the car never moves in the same tick that its doors are open.

blocks.title: An elevator ticking through its states

blocks.html:
Who decides which stop comes first? Put that decision in its own object, a policy with one method, choose(floor, direction, requests). The elevator just asks it. Then you can swap policies without touching the elevator. This is the strategy pattern.

Two policies to compare:

  • FIFO (first in, first out): go to whoever pressed first. Simple, but blind to where the car already is.
  • SCAN (the "elevator algorithm"): keep going in your current direction and stop at every request on the way; turn around only when nothing is left ahead.

blocks.title: scan_policy
blocks.prompt:
Write the Scan policy. choose(floor, direction, requests) returns (target, direction):

  • No requests: (None, direction).
  • "Ahead" means r >= floor when going "up", or r <= floor when going "down".
  • If nothing is ahead, flip the direction; then everything left is ahead.
  • Pick the nearest request among those ahead.
blocks.tests:
s = Scan()
assert s.choose(4, "up", [2, 7, 5]) == (5, "up"), f"going up from 4: the nearest request above is 5, got {s.choose(4, 'up', [2, 7, 5])}"
assert s.choose(4, "up", [2, 1]) == (2, "down"), "nothing above 4: turn around and take the nearest below"
assert s.choose(4, "down", [4, 9]) == (4, "down"), "a request on the current floor counts as ahead"
assert s.choose(0, "up", []) == (None, "up"), "no requests: no target"
assert Fifo().choose(4, "up", [2, 7]) == (2, "up"), "FIFO is unchanged: just the first request"
hints: Build the ahead list with a comprehension. If it's empty, flip direction and use all the requests.
min(ahead, key=lambda r: abs(r - floor)) picks the nearest one.

blocks.html: Now race them on the same burst from the simulation. The simulate function only ever talks to policy.choose, so it works with any policy object, including ones you haven't written yet.

blocks.title: FIFO vs SCAN on the same burst

blocks.q: You want to try a third policy, "nearest request first". What has to change?

opts.t: The Elevator class and the simulate function
Every policy class, so they agree on a new interface
Only a new class with a choose method; nothing else changes
Nothing; Python picks the best policy automatically

blocks.why: That's the payoff of the strategy pattern: simulate (and the elevator) only depend on "something with a choose method". A new policy is one new class plugged in.

blocks.html: The same moves you just made (find the objects, decide who owns which data, pull the decision into a swappable policy) work for almost any system: a parking garage, a ride-share dispatcher, a print queue.

blocks.title: Parking garage: levels, spots and an assignment policy
blocks.client: A city-centre car park that wants to stop drivers circling for spaces
blocks.brief: The garage has several levels, each with numbered spots. When a car arrives, the system assigns a spot and remembers which plate is where; when it leaves, the spot is freed. Management wants to try different assignment rules (fill the lowest level first, or spread cars out) without rewriting the system.
blocks.why: This is object modeling as it's done in real back-ends: ride-share dispatch (Rider, Driver, Trip, matching policy), warehouse robots (Shelf, Robot, picking policy), and cloud schedulers (Machine, Job, placement policy) all separate the things from the decision, so the decision can be tuned and A/B-tested.

Write a Garage that parks and frees cars through methods only
Make the spot choice a policy object with one pick(free_spots) method
Raise a clear error when the garage is full or a plate is unknown
Compare two policies by how far drivers walk (or drive) on average
stretch: Add spot sizes (motorbike, car, van) and only assign spots that fit
Add a second entrance and a policy that picks the spot nearest to it
Charge by the hour: add a Ticket object that remembers the arrival time

blocks.title: garage
blocks.prompt:
Write Garage(levels, spots_per_level, policy).

  • park(plate) asks policy.pick(free) for a spot, where free is a sorted list of (level, spot) tuples that are empty; it records the plate there and returns the tuple. Raise ValueError("full") if nothing is free.
  • leave(plate) frees that plate's spot and returns it. Unknown plate: raise KeyError.
  • free_count() returns how many spots are empty.
hints: Store a dict {(level, spot): plate_or_None} for the spots and a second dict {plate: (level, spot)} so leave is instant.
free_spots() is sorted(k for k, v in self._spots.items() if v is None). Hand that list to self._policy.pick(...).

blocks.title: scan_elevator
blocks.prompt:
From memory: write an Elevator(floor=0) that runs the SCAN policy as a state machine.

  • call(floor) adds a stop (ignore duplicates).
  • tick() returns the new state: doors open → "IDLE"; no stops → "IDLE"; at a stop → remove it, append it to self.served, "DOORS_OPEN"; otherwise move one floor toward the SCAN target (add 1 to self.travelled), "MOVING_UP" or "MOVING_DOWN".
  • The car starts with direction "up".
blocks.tests:
e = Elevator(0)
e.call(5); e.call(2)
for _ in range(50):
    e.tick()
assert e.served == [2, 5], f"going up from 0, SCAN stops at 2 on the way to 5; served {e.served}"
assert e.travelled == 5, f"0 to 5 is 5 floors, got {e.travelled}"
e = Elevator(3)
e.call(5); e.call(1); e.call(4); e.call(4)
for _ in range(50):
    e.tick()
assert e.served == [4, 5, 1], f"from 3 going up: 4, 5, then turn around for 1; served {e.served}"
assert e.travelled == 6, "3→5 is 2 floors, 5→1 is 4 more"
f = Elevator(0); f.call(1)
assert f.tick() == "MOVING_UP" and f.tick() == "DOORS_OPEN" and f.tick() == "IDLE", "move, open, then close"
hints: Keep the SCAN choice in a helper method. tick() is then the four-state rule from earlier, plus moving one floor.

blocks.q: Why make the scheduling policy its own object instead of writing the FIFO or SCAN logic inside the Elevator class?
blocks.a: Because "how do I move" and "where should I go next" are different responsibilities. With the policy as a separate object that has one method (choose), the elevator only asks it for a target, so you can swap FIFO for SCAN (or a new policy) without editing or re-testing the elevator, and compare them fairly on the same inputs. That's the strategy pattern; composition lets the Building plug in whichever policy it wants.

chapters.title: A calculator
chapters.tagline: Characters become tokens, tokens become a tree, the tree becomes one number
goals: Split a string like 12+3*(4-1) into tokens with a small scanner
Explain why precedence is the shape of a tree, not a rule you memorise
Write a recursive-descent parser with one function per precedence level
Evaluate a tree bottom-up, and make errors point at the real mistake
Use the same engine to power spreadsheet formulas

blocks.html:
Type 2+3*4 into your phone and you get 14, not 20. Somewhere inside, the calculator decided the * goes first. How?

It doesn't read left to right. It runs three small machines, one after another:

  1. Tokenizer: characters → words ("12" is one number, not two digits).
  2. Parser: words → a tree. Operators that bind tightly sit deeper.
  3. Evaluator: the tree → one number, starting from the leaves.

Play with all three before writing any code.

blocks.name: bx-calc
blocks.title: Tokens, tree, answer
blocks.goal: Find an expression where reading left to right gives a different answer than the tree. Press Run all to compare.
blocks.intro: Press Step and watch which operator runs first. Then click an operator block: it tells you why it sits where it does.

blocks.q: In the tree for 2+3*4, which operator is at the very top (the root)?

opts.t: *, because it runs first
+, because it runs last
Neither; the root is always a number
It depends on the order you type it

blocks.why: The root is computed last: it needs both children finished first. + binds loosely, so it ends up on top, and * sits underneath it.

blocks.html: A token is the smallest meaningful piece: a number, an operator or a bracket. The tokenizer walks the string one character at a time. When it sees a digit, it keeps going while the next character is also a digit, so 12 becomes one token.

blocks.code:
src = "12+3"
tokens = []
i = 0
while i < len(src):
    if src[i].isdigit():
        j = i
        while j < len(src) and src[j].isdigit():
            j += 1
        tokens.append(src[i:j])
        i = j
    else:
        tokens.append(src[i])
        i += 1
print(tokens)
print(len(tokens))

blocks.title: tokenize
blocks.prompt: Write tokenize(src) that returns a list of tokens. Numbers become floats (allow a decimal point, like 3.5), operators and brackets stay as one-character strings, and spaces are skipped. Any other character should raise ValueError with a message that says which character it was.
blocks.tests:
assert tokenize("12+3") == [12.0, "+", 3.0], f"'12+3' should give [12.0, '+', 3.0], got {tokenize('12+3')}"
assert tokenize(" 2 * ( 3.5 - 1 ) ") == [2.0, "*", "(", 3.5, "-", 1.0, ")"], "spaces are skipped and 3.5 is one number"
assert tokenize("2^10") == [2.0, "^", 10.0], "^ is an operator"
try:
    tokenize("2 $ 3")
    assert False, "'$' should raise ValueError"
except ValueError as e:
    assert "$" in str(e), "the error message should name the bad character"

Remember to set i = j after reading a number, otherwise you'll read the same digits again.

sections.title: Precedence is the shape of the tree

blocks.html:
Here is the trick that makes * go first without any special case: write one function per precedence level, and let the loosest level call the tighter one.

  • expr() handles + and -. To get its operands it calls…
  • term(), which handles * and /. To get its operands it calls…
  • factor(), which reads a number or a whole ( … ) group.

Because term() finishes building 3*4 before expr() ever sees the +, the multiplication ends up deeper in the tree. This style is called recursive descent, and real compilers (GCC, Clang, Go, V8) use it.

We'll store a tree as nested tuples: a number is just a float, and an operation is (op, left, right). So 2+3*4 is ("+", 2.0, ("*", 3.0, 4.0)).

blocks.title: The term level of the parser
parse
blocks.prompt: The parser is almost done. Fill the two blanks in expr and factor. expr loops over +/- using term for each side; factor reads either a number or a bracketed sub-expression.
hints: The right-hand side of a + is a whole term, so it can contain its own *. And inside brackets, anything can appear, so start again from the loosest level.

blocks.html: Evaluation is the easy part, and it's recursive: a number is its own value; an operation evaluates its left child, then its right child, then combines them. The recursion naturally goes to the deepest node first, which is why the tree's shape decides the order.

blocks.code:
def ev(t):
    if isinstance(t, float):
        return t
    op, a, b = t
    x, y = ev(a), ev(b)
    print("compute", x, op, y)
    return x + y if op == "+" else x * y

print(ev(("+", 2.0, ("*", 3.0, 4.0))))

blocks.title: evaluate
blocks.prompt: Write evaluate(tree) for trees made of floats and (op, left, right) tuples, with op one of + - * / ^. Dividing by zero should raise ZeroDivisionError (Python does that for you).
blocks.tests:
assert evaluate(5.0) == 5.0, "a number evaluates to itself"
assert evaluate(("+", 2.0, ("*", 3.0, 4.0))) == 14.0, "2+3*4 = 14"
assert evaluate(("-", ("-", 8.0, 3.0), 2.0)) == 3.0, "(8-3)-2 = 3"
assert evaluate(("^", 2.0, 10.0)) == 1024.0, "2^10 = 1024"
try:
    evaluate(("/", 1.0, 0.0)); assert False, "dividing by zero should raise"
except ZeroDivisionError:
    pass
hints: Start with the base case: if isinstance(tree, (int, float)): return float(tree). Otherwise unpack op, a, b = tree and evaluate both sides first.
blocks.solution:
def evaluate(tree):
    if isinstance(tree, (int, float)):
        return float(tree)
    op, a, b = tree
    x, y = evaluate(a), evaluate(b)
    if op == "+": return x + y
    if op == "-": return x - y
    if op == "*": return x * y
    if op == "/": return x / y
    if op == "^": return x ** y
    raise ValueError(f"unknown operator {op}")

blocks.html: A good calculator doesn't just say "error". It says where. This version runs, but its message about a missing number is wrong.

sections.title: Real-world project: a spreadsheet formula engine

blocks.html: Every spreadsheet (Excel, Google Sheets, Numbers) has exactly the machine you just built at its core. A cell like =A1*2+B1 is tokenized, parsed into a tree and evaluated, except some leaves are cell names that you look up.

blocks.title: Mini spreadsheet: formulas that reference other cells
blocks.client: A small bakery tracking costs in a sheet
blocks.brief: The bakery's sheet has cells like A1 = 2.5 (flour price), A2 = 4 (bags) and A3 = A1*A2 (total). Change the flour price and the total must update. Your job: extend your calculator so a leaf can be a cell name, and evaluating it means evaluating that cell's formula.
blocks.why: This is how spreadsheets, build systems (a target depends on other targets) and reactive UI frameworks (a value depends on other values) all work: a dependency graph evaluated on demand. Spotting a cycle (A1 = A2, A2 = A1) is the same check make does.

blocks.prompt: Write cell_value(sheet, name). sheet maps cell names to either a number or a formula string like "A1*A2+1". Use the provided tokenize_cells (which returns cell names as strings like "A1") and parse (a working parser whose leaves are floats or cell-name strings). blocks.title: calc
blocks.prompt: From memory: write calc(src) that tokenizes, parses (with + - looser than * /, and brackets) and evaluates a string. No peeking at the steps above.
hints: You can evaluate while you parse: have expr, term and factor return numbers instead of trees.

blocks.q: In your own words: why does 2+3*4 give 14 in your calculator, even though nothing in the code says "do multiplication first"?
blocks.a: Because the parser has one function per precedence level, and the + level gets its operands by calling the * level. So 3*4 is completely built (and becomes a subtree) before the + is combined. Evaluation is bottom-up, so deeper nodes are computed first. Precedence is the shape of the tree.

chapters.title: A math engine
chapters.tagline: Variables, derivatives by rule, and why a computer algebra system must simplify
goals: Evaluate an expression tree that contains variables, using an environment
Turn each derivative rule (sum, product, power, chain) into a few lines of recursion
Explain why a derivative tree explodes without simplification, and write a simplifier
Check symbolic derivatives against numbers with a finite difference
Use your own derivatives to find a best price with Newton's method

blocks.html:
In chapter 2 every leaf of the tree was a number. Let one leaf be the letter x and you have a math engine: the thing inside Wolfram Alpha, SymPy, and the autograd of every deep-learning library.

The big surprise: differentiation is just another tree walk. Each rule (sum, product, chain) only looks at the top node of a tree and says what to build. Recursion handles everything below. The catch is that the rules produce a lot of junk like 1*cos(x) and 0*x, and if nobody cleans it up, the tree grows out of control.

blocks.name: bx-symdiff
blocks.title: Grow a derivative, rule by rule
blocks.goal: Differentiate something that needs the product or chain rule, with Simplify: on, so the result ends up smaller than the raw derivative.
blocks.intro: Pick x*sin(x) and press Differentiate a few times. Each new block is tagged with the rule that made it. Then flip Simplify and compare the node counts.

blocks.q: The derivative rules produce ("*", 1.0, ("cos", "x")). Why bother simplifying it to ("cos", "x"), if both give the same numbers?

opts.t: It's only for looks; the computer doesn't care
Every extra node gets copied and differentiated again next time, so junk multiplies with each derivative
Python can't evaluate a tree that contains 1.0
The product rule only works on simplified trees

blocks.why: Both trees give the same value, but the second derivative of the unsimplified one has to differentiate the 1.0 and the * too, producing even more junk. Simplifying keeps the tree small, which keeps everything after it fast.

blocks.html:
Our trees use the same shapes as the calculator: a number is a float, an operation is a tuple like ("+", a, b). Two new things:

  • a variable is a string leaf, like "x";
  • a function is a tuple with one child, like ("sin", "x").

To evaluate a tree with variables you need to know what each variable is worth right now. That lookup table is called an environment: a dict like {"x": 2.0}. Every interpreter has one; in Python, it's what globals() returns.

blocks.code:
def evaluate(t, env):
    if isinstance(t, float):
        return t
    if isinstance(t, str):
        return env[t]
    op, a, b = t
    x, y = evaluate(a, env), evaluate(b, env)
    return x + y if op == "+" else x * y

tree = ("+", ("*", "x", "x"), 1.0)
print(evaluate(tree, {"x": 3.0}))
print(evaluate(tree, {"x": -2.0}))

blocks.title: evaluate
blocks.prompt: Write evaluate(t, env) for trees made of floats, variable names (strings looked up in env), binary operations ("+" | "-" | "*" | "/" | "^", a, b) and functions ("sin" | "cos" | "exp", a). Use math.sin, math.cos, math.exp.
blocks.tests:
assert evaluate(("+", ("*", "x", "x"), 1.0), {"x": 3.0}) == 10.0, "x*x + 1 at x=3 is 10"
assert evaluate(("^", "x", 3.0), {"x": 2.0}) == 8.0, "x^3 at 2 is 8"
assert abs(evaluate(("sin", ("*", 2.0, "x")), {"x": 0.25}) - math.sin(0.5)) < 1e-12, "sin(2x) at 0.25 is sin(0.5)"
assert evaluate(("*", "a", "b"), {"a": 4.0, "b": 2.5}) == 10.0, "any variable name works, not just x"

sections.title: Each rule only looks at the top

blocks.html:
Here is every rule you need, written as "what to build". d(u) means "the derivative of u", which is a recursive call.

The tree is…Its derivative is…Name
a number c0constant
x1 (and any other variable gives 0)
u + vd(u) + d(v)sum
u * vd(u)*v + u*d(v)product
u ^ n (n a number)n u^(n-1) d(u)power + chain
sin(u)cos(u) * d(u)chain

Notice the * d(u) at the end of the last two. That's the chain rule: whatever is inside the function changes too, and its rate of change multiplies in. Forgetting it is the most common calculus mistake there is, and the recursion makes it impossible to forget.

Every rule for a function or a power ends with deriv(u, v) (or deriv(a, v)) multiplied in: that's the chain rule.

blocks.html: Let's count nodes. Each derivative copies the original subtrees and adds new ones, so sizes grow fast, and the junk (*1.0, +0.0) gets differentiated again next time.

blocks.title: Derivatives of derivatives, unsimplified

blocks.html:
A simplifier walks the tree bottom-up (simplify the children first, then look at the node) and applies safe rewrites:

  • both children are numbers → compute it now (constant folding);
  • u*0 or 0*u → 0; u*1 or 1*u → u;
  • u+0 or 0+u → u; u-0 → u;
  • u^1 → u; u^0 → 1.

blocks.html: How do you know your rules are right? Ask the definition of a derivative directly: nudge x a tiny bit and see how much f moves. The central difference (f(x+h) - f(x-h)) / 2h is a numeric slope that needs no rules at all. If your symbolic derivative disagrees with it, a rule is wrong. Every autodiff library tests itself exactly this way ("gradient checking").

h = 1e-3

blocks.title: max_error
blocks.prompt: Write max_error(t, xs, h=1e-5): for each x in xs, compare evaluate(deriv(t), {"x": x}) with the central difference of evaluate(t, ...), and return the largest absolute difference. evaluate and deriv are defined (and correct).
blocks.tests:

assert 0 < e < 1e-6, f"a correct derivative agrees with the numbers to about 1e-9; got {e}"
assert max_error(("^", "x", 4.0), [3.0]) < 1e-4, "x^4 at 3: exact 108, the difference agrees"
hints: d = deriv(t) once, then loop: the exact value is evaluate(d, {"x": x}), the numeric one uses x + h and x - h.
blocks.solution:
def max_error(t, xs, h=1e-5):
    worst = 0.0
    d = deriv(t)
    for x in xs:
        exact = evaluate(d, {"x": x})
        approx = (evaluate(t, {"x": x + h}) - evaluate(t, {"x": x - h})) / (2 * h)
        worst = max(worst, abs(exact - approx))
    return worst

blocks.q: Explain to a friend why a computer can differentiate any formula with just a handful of rules, and why it then has to simplify.
blocks.a: Every formula is a tree, and each rule only needs to know the top node (a sum, a product, a sin) plus the derivatives of the children, which it gets by calling itself. Recursion walks the whole tree, so a few rules cover everything. But the rules are mechanical: they produce *1, +0 and repeated copies of subtrees. Without simplification those leftovers are carried and differentiated again, so the tree (and the time to evaluate it) grows explosively.

chapters.tagline: Patterns become a machine of states, and running every path at once keeps it fast
goals: Match literal text, ., * and ? with a small recursive backtracking matcher

sections.title: What a regex engine really does

blocks.html:
A regular expression (regex) is a tiny language for describing text. ab*c means "an a, then any number of bs, then a c". Every editor's search box, every signup form that checks an email, and every log tool like grep runs a regex engine.

There are two ways to build one:

  1. Backtracking: try one choice, and if it fails later, go back and try the other. Easy to write. Python's re, JavaScript and Perl work this way.
  2. State machine (NFA): turn the pattern into a little machine of states and arrows, then walk the text once while keeping track of every state you could be in. grep, RE2 and Rust's regex work this way.

Both give the same answers. The difference is how many steps they take. Play first:

blocks.name: bx-regex
blocks.title: Pattern → state machine, text → one character at a time
blocks.goal: Find a pattern and text where backtracking takes at least 10× more steps than the NFA. Try the slider.
blocks.intro: Each block in the middle is a state. Blue arrows read one character; grey arrows are free moves. Press Step to consume one character and watch which states light up. Click any block to ask why it's there.

blocks.q: The NFA simulation lights up several states at once. What does a lit state mean?

opts.t: The engine has already matched the whole pattern
"After reading the text so far, the pattern could be at this point"
The state has been visited before and is now forbidden
The state is waiting for the backtracker to return to it

blocks.why: A set of lit states is a list of all the places the pattern could be right now. Instead of guessing one path and backing up, the NFA keeps every possible path alive at the same time.

blocks.html:
Start with the smallest possible regex: literal text. The pattern cat matches the text cat, and nothing else. Comparing character by character is enough.

Add one special character: . means "any single character". So c.t matches cat, cot and c9t. The only change is the comparison: a pattern character matches if it is equal or it is a dot.

In this chapter, match means the whole text must match (like re.fullmatch). We'll make it "find anywhere" at the end, for grep.

That works because each pattern character eats exactly one text character. The moment we add * ("zero or more of the previous thing"), that's no longer true: ab*c can match a text of length 2 or 200. We need a different shape of code.

sections.title: Star and question mark: try, and back up

blocks.html:
Here is the idea, written as a recursive function. Look at the start of the pattern:

  • If it's x*: either use the star zero times (skip x* and keep going), or, if the first text character matches x, eat it and stay on x* to maybe eat more.
  • If it's x?: either eat one x, or skip it.
  • Otherwise: the first characters must match, then match the rest.

The or is the important part: if the first choice fails later, Python comes back and tries the second. That "coming back" is backtracking.

blocks.title: The backtracking matcher for literals, . and *
blocks.tests:
assert match("ab*c", "ac"), "b* can be used zero times"
assert match("ab*c", "abbbc"), "b* can eat many b's"
assert not match("ab*c", "abd"), "the d doesn't match c"
assert match(".*", "anything"), ".* matches anything"
lines: return match(p[2:], t) or (first and match(p, t[1:]))
distractors: return match(p[2:], t) and (first and match(p, t[1:]))

blocks.title: match_with_optional
blocks.prompt: Add ? to the matcher. x? means "one x or nothing". Fill in the blank: try eating one character first (if it matches), and if that whole attempt fails, try skipping x?.
blocks.tests:
assert match("colou?r", "color"), "u? can be skipped: colou?r matches color"
assert match("colou?r", "colour"), "u? can eat one u: colou?r matches colour"
assert not match("colou?r", "colouur"), "? means at most ONE"
assert match("a?b", "b") and match("a?b", "ab"), "a?b matches b and ab"
assert match("ab*c?", "abb"), "c? at the end can be skipped"
hints: Eating one character means: first must be true, then match the rest of the pattern after x? (p[2:]) against the rest of the text (t[1:]).
Skipping means: match p[2:] against the same t. Join the two attempts with or.

blocks.html:
Backtracking is simple, but each or can make the work double. Most of the time the first choice succeeds and nobody notices. Now try a nasty pattern: a? repeated n times, then a repeated n times, on a text of n as.

The greedy matcher eats an a for every a?, runs out of text before the required as, backs up one choice, fails again, backs up two… It tries almost every combination of "eat / skip" for the n question marks: about 2ⁿ of them.

blocks.title: Count the calls

blocks.html: Each extra a? roughly doubles the calls. At n = 30 it would be about a billion calls; at n = 40 your laptop would still be working tomorrow. This is a real attack called ReDoS (regular expression denial of service): in 2019 one bad regex took down Cloudflare's whole network for 27 minutes.
The fix is not a faster computer. It is a different idea: never choose. Keep every possibility alive at once. To do that we first need the pattern as a proper structure.

sections.title: Groups and `|`: parse the pattern into a tree

blocks.html:
Real patterns have | ("or") and brackets: (cat|dog)s?. That's an expression language with precedence, just like the calculator:

  • | binds loosest (like +),
  • putting things next to each other (concatenation) is next (like *),
  • * and ? bind tightest, to the single thing before them,
  • ( … ) groups, like brackets in maths.

So we reuse recursive descent: one function per level. The tree uses tuples: ("char", "a"), ("cat", A, B), ("alt", A, B), ("star", A), ("opt", A).

blocks.code:
def parse_regex(src):
    pos = 0
    def peek():
        return src[pos] if pos < len(src) else None
    def alt():                       # loosest:  A | B
        nonlocal pos
        node = cat()
        while peek() == "|":
            pos += 1
            node = ("alt", node, cat())
        return node
    def cat():                       # middle:   A B C
        node = None
        while peek() not in (None, "|", ")"):
            r = rep()
            node = r if node is None else ("cat", node, r)
        return node if node is not None else ("empty",)
    def rep():                       # tightest: A*  A?
        nonlocal pos
        node = atom()
        while peek() in ("*", "?"):
            node = ("star" if peek() == "*" else "opt", node)
            pos += 1
        return node
    def atom():                      # a letter, a dot, or ( ... )
        nonlocal pos
        c = peek()
        pos += 1
        if c == "(":
            node = alt()
            if peek() != ")":
                raise ValueError("a ( is never closed")
            pos += 1
            return node
        return ("char", c)
    tree = alt()
    if pos != len(src):
        raise ValueError(f"unexpected {src[pos]!r} at {pos}")
    return tree

print(parse_regex("ab*"))
print(parse_regex("cat|dog"))
print(parse_regex("(ab)*"))
blocks.title: A regex parser (same shape as the calculator's)

blocks.html: Notice ab* became cat(a, star(b)): the star grabbed only the b, because rep() is deeper than cat(). Precedence is the shape of the tree, exactly like 2+3*4.

In 1968 Ken Thompson (who later co-created Unix) turned regex trees into machines. A machine is a set of numbered states joined by arrows. An arrow either reads one character, or is a free move (None: you may take it without reading anything).

Every piece of the tree becomes a small machine with one start and one end, and bigger pieces just wire smaller ones together:

  • char c: start →c→ end.
  • cat A B: A's end →free→ B's start.
  • alt A B: a new start with free moves into A and into B; both ends free-move to a new end.
  • star A: a new start that can free-move into A or skip straight to the end; A's end can free-move back to A's start (go round again) or to the end.
  • opt A: like star, without the loop back.

Why one start and one end? Because then every piece plugs into every other piece the same way, like LEGO.

blocks.title: thompson_build
blocks.prompt: build(nfa, node) returns (start, end) for a tree node. The char and cat cases work. Fill in the four missing arrows of star: the new start can enter A or skip to the end; A's end can loop back to A's start or leave to the end. Use nfa.add(from, None, to) for a free move.

assert ok(ab_star, "abbb"), "ab* must match 'abbb': A's end must loop back to A's start"

Skipping and leaving both go to e. Entering and going round both go to a_start.
blocks.starter:
def build(nfa, node):
    kind = node[0]
    if kind == "char":
        s, e = nfa.new(), nfa.new()
        nfa.add(s, node[1], e)
        return s, e
    if kind == "cat":
        s1, e1 = build(nfa, node[1])
        s2, e2 = build(nfa, node[2])
        nfa.add(e1, None, s2)
        return s1, e2
    if kind == "star":
        s, e = nfa.new(), nfa.new()
        a_start, a_end = build(nfa, node[1])
        nfa.add(s, None, ____)        # enter A
        nfa.add(s, None, ____)        # skip A completely (zero times)
        nfa.add(a_end, None, ____)    # go round again
        nfa.add(a_end, None, ____)    # leave
        return s, e
blocks.solution:
def build(nfa, node):
    kind = node[0]
    if kind == "char":
        s, e = nfa.new(), nfa.new()
        nfa.add(s, node[1], e)
        return s, e
    if kind == "cat":
        s1, e1 = build(nfa, node[1])
        s2, e2 = build(nfa, node[2])
        nfa.add(e1, None, s2)
        return s1, e2
    if kind == "star":
        s, e = nfa.new(), nfa.new()
        a_start, a_end = build(nfa, node[1])
        nfa.add(s, None, a_start)
        nfa.add(s, None, e)
        nfa.add(a_end, None, a_start)
        nfa.add(a_end, None, e)
        return s, e

sections.title: Run every path at once: the state set

blocks.html:
Now the trick that kills the explosion. Keep a set of the states you could be in:

  1. Start with {start}, plus everything reachable from it by free moves. That "plus free moves" is called the closure.
  2. For each character of the text: follow every arrow labelled with that character (or .) from any state in the set. That gives the next set. Take its closure.
  3. At the end, it matched if the end state is in the set.

A state is in the set at most once, however many paths lead to it. So each character costs at most "number of states" work. For a pattern of m states and a text of n characters that's at most m × n steps: it grows linearly, never 2ⁿ.

sections.title: Real-world project: a mini grep for log files

blocks.html: grep prints every line of a file that contains a match. "Contains" is the new part: the pattern may start anywhere in the line. With a state set that's a one-line change: at every character, also add the start state (and its closure) to the active set, as if a new attempt began there. And instead of waiting for the end, stop as soon as end shows up.

blocks.title: loggrep: search a server log with your own regex engine
blocks.client: An on-call engineer at a small web shop whose site is slow
blocks.brief: The web server writes lines like 2026-11-01 12:00:03 GET /cart 500 812ms. The engineer wants to type loggrep "GET /cart 5.." server.log and see every failing cart request, fast, even on a 2 GB log. Build it on your parser and NFA: parse the pattern once, compile it once, then stream lines through the state-set search.
blocks.why: This is literally what grep, ripgrep, RE2 (Google) and Rust's regex crate do, and why they promise linear time: they will never hang on a pathological pattern. Log search tools (Splunk, Loki, Elastic) and code search (GitHub) rely on the same guarantee, because users type arbitrary patterns.

Write search(nfa, start, end, line) that finds a match anywhere in the line
Write grep(pattern, lines) returning (line_number, line) for every hit
Read a real file line by line with open(...) and print the hits with their numbers
Add a -v option that prints lines that do not match

Add + (one or more): it's A A*, or a star without the skip arrow
Cache state sets you've seen before as single states: you've just invented a DFA, the fastest regex engines of all

blocks.title: grep
blocks.prompt: Using the provided compile_pattern(pattern) (returns nfa, start, end) and closure, write search(nfa, start, end, line) that returns True if the pattern matches anywhere in line, and grep(pattern, lines) that returns a list of (line_number, line) (numbers start at 1) for every matching line. Compile the pattern only once.
blocks.tests:
log = [
    "2026-11-01 12:00:01 GET /home 200 31ms",
    "2026-11-01 12:00:03 GET /cart 500 812ms",
    "2026-11-01 12:00:04 POST /cart 200 44ms",
    "2026-11-01 12:00:09 GET /cart 503 1200ms",
]
nfa, s, e = compile_pattern("cart 5")
assert search(nfa, s, e, log[1]), "'cart 5' appears in the middle of line 2: search must try every starting position"
assert not search(nfa, s, e, log[2]), "line 3 has 'cart 2', not 'cart 5'"
assert grep("GET /cart 5..", log) == [(2, log[1]), (4, log[3])], f"two failing cart GETs, on lines 2 and 4; got {grep('GET /cart 5..', log)}"
assert grep("POST|home", log) == [(1, log[0]), (3, log[2])], "| works inside grep"
assert grep("zzz", log) == [], "no hits gives an empty list"
COMPILES = 0
grep("ms", log)
assert COMPILES == 1, f"compile the pattern once per grep call, not once per line (compiled {COMPILES} times)"

Return True the moment end is in the active set: you don't need the match to reach the end of the line.

blocks.title: regex_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: write fullmatch(pattern, text) that supports literal characters, ., * and ? (each applying to the single character before it) and returns whether the whole text matches. Any approach is fine, but it must finish the evil test below quickly, so plain backtracking won't do: use a set of positions in the pattern (a state set) instead.
blocks.tests:
assert fullmatch("abc", "abc") and not fullmatch("abc", "abd"), "literal text"
assert fullmatch("a.c", "axc"), ". matches any character"
assert fullmatch("ab*c", "ac") and fullmatch("ab*c", "abbbbc"), "b* means zero or more b"
assert fullmatch("colou?r", "color") and fullmatch("colou?r", "colour"), "u? means zero or one u"
assert not fullmatch("ab*", "abx"), "the whole text must match"
t0 = time.perf_counter()
assert fullmatch("a?" * 30 + "a" * 30, "a" * 30), "(a?)^30 a^30 matches 30 a's"
assert time.perf_counter() - t0 < 2, "the evil pattern must be fast: keep a SET of pattern positions instead of backtracking"
hints: Let a "state" be an index into the pattern. Being at index i means "the next thing to match is pattern[i]".
Free moves: if pattern[i+1] is or ?, you may jump to i + 2 without reading anything. Reading a character on x keeps you at i.
blocks.starter:
def fullmatch(pattern, text):
    pass

blocks.q: Why can a backtracking regex engine take 2ⁿ steps on a?a?…a?aa…a, while an NFA simulation with a set of states stays fast?
blocks.a: Backtracking follows one path at a time; every ? is a choice, and when a later part fails it goes back and tries the other branch, so it can end up trying every combination of choices (2ⁿ). The NFA simulation never chooses: it keeps a set of all states the pattern could be in. A state is in the set at most once no matter how many paths reach it, so each text character costs at most (number of states) work: m × n in total.

chapters.title: A key-value database
chapters.tagline: An append-only log, a hash index of byte offsets, compaction and crash recovery
goals: Explain why a dict in memory is not a database, and why rewriting a whole file on every write is too slow
Store writes in an append-only log and read them back by scanning
Add an in-memory hash index of byte offsets (the Bitcask design) so a read touches one record
Delete with tombstones and keep the log small with compaction
Rebuild the index after a crash by replaying the log, and use checksums to throw away torn writes

sections.title: What a key-value database really does

blocks.html:
A key-value store is the simplest database there is: set(key, value), get(key), delete(key). That's the whole interface. Redis, Memcached, DynamoDB, RocksDB and the storage engine under many bigger databases all start from it.

The interface is easy. The hard part is the promise behind it: after set returns, the value survives a crash, and reads and writes stay fast even after millions of them. The design you'll build is called Bitcask (it powered the Riak database): a log on disk that only ever grows at the end, plus a small map in memory that remembers where each key's latest record is.

blocks.name: bx-kvlog
blocks.title: An append-only log with a hash index
blocks.goal: Write until a segment needs compaction, press Compact, then press Crash and watch the index come back by replaying the log.
blocks.intro: The long rows are the log on disk: every record is a block, coloured by its key. The blocks above are the index in memory: each points at its key's latest record. Click any block to ask why it's there.

blocks.q: In this design, what happens on disk when you set a key that already exists?

opts.t: The old record is found and overwritten in place
A new record is appended at the end; the old one stays until compaction
The whole file is rewritten with the new value
Nothing: values only live in memory until shutdown

blocks.why: Writes only ever append. Overwriting in place would mean finding the old record and maybe moving everything after it if the value grew. Appending is the fastest thing a disk can do, and the index simply moves its pointer to the new record.

blocks.html:
The obvious first try: a Python dict. Reads and writes are instant. But a dict lives in the process's memory. When the process crashes, or the machine loses power, it's gone.

So write it to a file. The obvious way is to save the whole dict every time something changes (like pressing Ctrl+S in an editor). It's correct, but count the bytes: every set rewrites everything, so the cost grows with the size of the database, not the size of the change.

In this chapter the "disk" is a bytearray: it behaves like a file you can append to and read slices of, and it runs anywhere.

blocks.code:
import json
db = {}
written = 0
for i in range(4):
    db[f"user{i}"] = "x" * 10
    data = json.dumps(db).encode()
    written += len(data)
    print(i, len(data), written)

blocks.html: Look at the last column. Writing four 10-byte values cost hundreds of bytes, and it gets worse every time: n writes cost roughly n²/2 record-sizes. A database with a million keys would rewrite gigabytes to change one value.

The fix: never touch old data. Every set appends one small record to the end of the log, like writing a new line in a diary. We'll use one line per record: key<TAB>value<NEWLINE>, as bytes.

Writes are now as cheap as they can be: you write exactly the new record. The cost moved to reads: to get a key you scan the whole log and keep the last record for that key (later records win, because they are newer).

blocks.title: append_and_scan
blocks.prompt: Write log_set(disk, key, value) that appends the record key\tvalue\n (encoded as UTF-8 bytes) to the bytearray disk, and log_get(disk, key) that scans every line and returns the value from the last record for that key, or None if there is none.
blocks.tests:
d = bytearray()
log_set(d, "cat", "meow")
assert bytes(d) == b"cat\tmeow\n", f"one record is key, tab, value, newline; got {bytes(d)!r}"
log_set(d, "dog", "woof")
log_set(d, "cat", "purr")
assert log_get(d, "cat") == "purr", "the LAST record for a key wins: it is the newest"
assert log_get(d, "dog") == "woof", "dog was written once"
assert log_get(d, "cow") is None, "a missing key gives None"
assert len(d) == 9 + 9 + 9, "appending never rewrites old records"
hints: disk += some_bytes appends in place to a bytearray. "text".encode() gives bytes.
For log_get, decode the whole disk, split("\n"), and keep overwriting a found variable whenever the key matches. Whatever is left at the end is the newest.

sections.title: A hash index of byte offsets

blocks.html:
Scanning is fine for ten records and hopeless for ten million. But notice: when we append a record, we know exactly where it starts: the length of the disk just before the append. Keep a dict in memory, index[key] = (offset, length), and a read becomes: look up the offset, read that one slice, done.

That's the Bitcask idea. Memory holds only the keys and two numbers each; the values stay on disk. Writes are still pure appends, and reads now touch exactly one record. The dict in memory is not the database any more; it's a map of the database, and (as you'll see) it can always be rebuilt from the log.

blocks.title: get with the index: read one record, not the whole log
blocks.setup:
disk = bytearray(b"a	1
b	22
a	333
")
index = {"a": (9, 6), "b": (4, 5)}
blocks.tests:
assert get(disk, index, "a") == "333", "index points at the newest record for a"
assert get(disk, index, "b") == "22", "b's record starts at byte 4"
assert get(disk, index, "z") is None, "a key not in the index is missing"

blocks.title: kv_with_index
blocks.prompt: Fill in the two blanks in set: remember where the record starts before appending it, then store (offset, length) in the index.
blocks.tests:
kv = KV()
kv.set("cat", "meow")
assert kv.index["cat"] == (0, 9), f"the first record starts at 0 and is 9 bytes; got {kv.index['cat']}"
for i in range(100):
    kv.set(f"k{i}", "v" * 50)
kv.set("cat", "purr")
assert kv.get("cat") == "purr", "get follows the index to the newest record"
assert kv.get("k7") == "v" * 50, "every key can be found"
kv.bytes_read = 0
kv.get("k42")
assert kv.bytes_read < 60, f"a get should read ONE record (~55 bytes), not the whole {len(kv.disk)}-byte log; read {kv.bytes_read}"
hints: Where does the next record start? Exactly at the current end of the disk.
The index value is a pair: (offset, len(record)).

blocks.html:
Two problems are left, and both come from "never touch old data".

Deletes. You can't erase a record from the middle of the log. Instead you append a tombstone: a record that says "this key is gone". We'll write it as just key\n (no tab). Reading the log later, a tombstone wins over older values just like a newer value would.

The log grows forever. Set the same key a thousand times and you have 999 dead records. So Bitcask splits the log into segments (files of a fixed size). When one is full it's closed and never written again, and a new one starts. Closed segments can be compacted in the background: copy only the live records (the newest per key, minus deleted keys) into a fresh segment, then throw the old ones away. Nothing reading the database notices, because the index is just switched to point at the new copies.

blocks.code:
import random
random.seed(1)
disk = bytearray()
latest = {}
for i in range(1000):
    key = f"user{random.randint(1, 50)}"
    rec = f"{key}\t{random.randint(0, 9999)}\n".encode()
    latest[key] = rec
    disk += rec
live = sum(len(r) for r in latest.values())
print(f"log size {len(disk)} bytes, live data {live} bytes")
print(f"{100 * (1 - live / len(disk)):.0f}% of the log is old versions nobody can read")
blocks.title: How much of the log is dead?
compact
blocks.prompt: Write compact(disk) that returns (new_disk, new_index): a new bytearray with only the newest record for each key (in the order of each key's first appearance in the old log), leaving out keys whose newest record is a tombstone (key\n), and the index {key: (offset, length)} for the new disk.
blocks.tests:
old = bytearray(b"a	1
b	2
a	3
c	4
b
a	5
")
new, idx = compact(old)
assert bytes(new) == b"a	5
c	4
", f"keep a's newest value (5), keep c, drop b (deleted); got {bytes(new)!r}"
assert idx == {"a": (0, 4), "c": (4, 4)}, f"the index must point into the NEW disk; got {idx}"
assert len(new) < len(old), "compaction shrinks the log"
assert compact(bytearray()) == (bytearray(), {}), "an empty log stays empty"
hints: First pass: walk the lines and fill a dict latest[key] = value (or None for a tombstone). Python dicts keep the order keys were first inserted, which is exactly the order the test wants.
Second pass: append each live record to a new bytearray, recording its offset before appending.

blocks.html:
Now pull the plug. Memory is wiped, so the index is gone. But the log is on disk, and the log is the truth: replay it from the start, and for every record set index[key] = (offset, length) (or remove the key for a tombstone). Afterwards the index is exactly what it was. That's crash recovery by replaying the log, and it's why "append only" is such a strong idea: there is never a half-updated structure on disk to repair.

Almost never. If the power dies while a record is being written, the end of the log holds a torn write: half a record. Worse, a disk can return garbage for a damaged block. So every record carries a checksum: a number computed from its bytes. On replay, recompute it; if it doesn't match, the record is broken, and so is everything after it, so stop there and cut the log off. The format becomes crc<TAB>key<TAB>value<NEWLINE>, where crc is zlib.crc32 of key\tvalue in 8 hex digits.

blocks.code:
import zlib
good = zlib.crc32(b"cat\tmeow")
print(f"{good:08x}")
damaged = zlib.crc32(b"cat\tmeom")
print(f"{damaged:08x}")
print(zlib.crc32(b"cat\tmeow") == good)

blocks.html: One wrong letter gives a completely different checksum. That's what makes it a good detector: random damage almost never produces a matching number.

blocks.title: recover_stops_at_torn_write
blocks.prompt: recover(disk) replays a checksummed log and returns (index, good_length), where good_length is where the last good record ends (the caller cuts the disk there). After a crash in the middle of a write, it returns the wrong good_length and trusts a broken record. Find and fix the bug.
blocks.tests:
disk = bytearray(record("cat", "meow") + record("dog", "woof"))
whole = len(disk)
idx, n = recover(disk)
assert n == whole and set(idx) == {"cat", "dog"}, "a clean log replays completely"
torn = disk + record("cat", "purr")[:9]          # the power died 9 bytes into a record
idx, n = recover(torn)
assert n == whole, f"a torn last record must be cut off: good length is {whole}, got {n}"
assert idx["cat"] == (0, len(record("cat", "meow"))), "cat must still point at its last GOOD record"
bad = bytearray(disk)
bad[12] = ord("X")                               # flip one byte inside the first record
idx, n = recover(bad)
assert n == 0 and idx == {}, "a record whose checksum doesn't match (and everything after it) can't be trusted"
hints: There are two ways a record can be broken: it never got its final \n, or its checksum doesn't match its body. In both cases, stop the loop.
To check: recompute f"{zlib.crc32(body.encode()):08x}" and compare it with the crc field.

sections.title: Real-world project: a URL shortener backend

blocks.title: tinylink: a URL shortener on your own storage engine
blocks.client: A school newsletter that prints links on paper
blocks.brief: Long links don't fit on a printed page. tinylink turns https://example.org/very/long/path?with=params into t.ly/3f and redirects anyone who visits it. Every new link is a set(code, url); every visit is a get(code). It has to survive restarts: a printed link must work for years. Build it on your KV store: the log on disk is the source of truth, and the index is rebuilt by replay at start-up.
blocks.why: URL shorteners (bit.ly), session stores (a login cookie → user id), shopping carts and feature flags are all key-value workloads: tiny records, lots of reads, a "latest value wins" rule. Bitcask itself was built for Riak; the same log + index + compaction pattern is inside Kafka, RocksDB's write-ahead log, PostgreSQL's WAL and every database that promises not to lose a committed write.
milestones: Wrap your KV store in a Shortener with shorten(url) and resolve(code)
Make short codes from a counter in base 62 (0-9a-zA-Z), so they stay short
Restore the counter after a restart by replaying the log, not by trusting memory
Return the existing code if the same URL is shortened twice (a second index: url → code)
Run compaction when more than half the log is dead records
stretch: Count visits per code without making the log explode (hint: batch the counters)
Add expiry: a link that stops working after 30 days (store the deadline in the value)
Serve it for real with http.server: GET /<code> replies with a 301 redirect

blocks.title: shortener
blocks.prompt: Using the provided KV (with set, get and a disk you can pass to KV(disk) to recover after a restart), write a Shortener class: Shortener(kv), shorten(url) returns a new code (base 62 of a counter starting at 1: "1", "2", … "z", "A", … "Z", "10", …) and stores code → url; resolve(code) returns the url or None. Store the counter in the KV too (under the key "#next") so a restarted Shortener keeps counting instead of reusing codes.
blocks.tests:
kv = KV()
s = Shortener(kv)
a = s.shorten("https://example.org/a")
b = s.shorten("https://example.org/b")
assert (a, b) == ("1", "2"), f"codes count up from 1 in base 62; got {a}, {b}"
assert s.resolve(a) == "https://example.org/a", "resolve returns the stored url"
assert s.resolve("zzz") is None, "an unknown code resolves to None"
for i in range(59):
    last = s.shorten(f"https://example.org/{i}")
assert last == "Z", f"the 61st link gets code 'Z' (61 is the last base-62 digit); got {last}"
assert s.shorten("https://example.org/next") == "10", "after Z comes 10, like after 9 in decimal"
s2 = Shortener(KV(kv.disk))            # restart: memory is gone, the log is replayed
assert s2.resolve("2") == "https://example.org/b", "links survive a restart"
assert s2.shorten("https://new.example") == "11", "after a restart the counter continues; it must not reuse code 1"
hints: Base 62 is like converting to decimal digits: n, r = divmod(n, 62) gives the last digit DIGITS[r]; repeat until n is 0.
In shorten, read the counter with int(self.kv.get("#next") or 1), use it, and set it back to n + 1. Because it lives in the log, replay restores it.

blocks.title: bitcask_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: write a class Store over a bytearray log with set(key, value), get(key) (via an in-memory index of (offset, length), returning None if missing), delete(key) (appends a tombstone key\n), and a constructor Store(disk=None) that rebuilds the index by replaying an existing log. Records are key\tvalue\n.
blocks.tests:
s = Store()
s.set("a", "1"); s.set("b", "2"); s.set("a", "3")
assert s.get("a") == "3" and s.get("b") == "2", "the newest value wins"
s.delete("b")
assert s.get("b") is None, "a deleted key is gone"
assert bytes(s.disk).endswith(b"b\n"), "delete appends a tombstone, it doesn't erase"
r = Store(s.disk)
assert r.get("a") == "3" and r.get("b") is None, "replaying the log after a crash rebuilds the same index, tombstones included"
assert r.index["a"] == s.index["a"], "replay points at the same offsets"
hints: Replay walks the records in order with a running offset; each line is len(line) + 1 bytes long (the newline).

blocks.q: In a Bitcask-style store, what is on disk, what is in memory, and why can you lose the memory part safely?
blocks.a: On disk: an append-only log of records (newest version wins, tombstones for deletes), split into segments that compaction rewrites to drop dead records. In memory: a hash index from each key to the byte offset (and length) of its newest record, so a read is one lookup plus one small disk read. The index is only a cache of where things are: after a crash you rebuild it by replaying the log from the start, and checksums let you detect and cut off a torn final write.

chapters.title: Git from scratch
chapters.tagline: Name every file by its fingerprint, and history becomes a graph of snapshots that share everything they can
goals: Explain why naming data by its SHA-1 hash gives free deduplication and tamper-evidence
Store blobs, trees and commits in a plain dictionary, exactly like git's object store
Treat branches and HEAD as movable pointers, and walk history by following parents
Diff two snapshots and find the merge base of two branches in the commit graph
Merge two branches file by file with a three-way merge, and spot real conflicts

blocks.html:
Most people picture git as "a list of changes". It isn't. Every commit is a full snapshot of your project. That sounds wasteful: 1,000 commits of a 1,000-file project would be a million files. Yet a .git folder is usually small.

The trick is one idea: name every piece of data by a fingerprint of its content. If a file didn't change, its fingerprint didn't change, so the new snapshot just points at the old copy. Nothing is stored twice.

There are only three kinds of object:

  1. Blob: the contents of one file.
  2. Tree: a folder, written as a list of name → blob id.
  3. Commit: a tree id, the id of the commit before it (its parent), and a message.

Play first. Each column is a commit (top), its tree (middle) and its file blobs (bottom).

blocks.name: bx-git
blocks.title: Snapshots that share what didn't change
blocks.goal: Make a branch, commit on both branches, then merge them into a commit with two parents.
blocks.intro: Edit one file and commit: only that file's blob, the tree and the commit get new ids. The other blobs are shared (lines back to the old blocks). Click any block to ask why.

blocks.q: You change one file out of three and commit. How many new objects does git store?

opts.t: 1: just the changed file
3: the new blob, a new tree (its list changed) and a new commit
5: three blobs, a tree and a commit
It stores the difference between the old and new file

blocks.why: The two untouched files keep their ids, so the new tree simply points at the old blobs. The tree itself is new because one of its lines changed, and the commit is new because it points at a new tree.

blocks.html:
A hash function turns any amount of data into a short fixed-size fingerprint. SHA-1 gives 40 hex characters. Two promises matter:

  • Same input → same hash, on every computer, forever.
  • Change one byte → a completely different hash. And nobody knows how to find two different files with the same SHA-1 by accident.

So the hash can be the file's name. That's called content addressing. Git hashes a small header (blob <length>, then a zero byte) followed by the content. This is exactly what git hash-object does.

blocks.code:
def oid(kind, body):
    data = f"{kind} {len(body)}\0{body}".encode()
    return hashlib.sha1(data).hexdigest()

print(oid("blob", "hello\n"))
print(oid("blob", "hello\n") == oid("blob", "hello\n"))
print(oid("blob", "Hello\n")[:12])
print(len(oid("blob", "a whole novel " * 1000)))

blocks.html: Two things fall out for free. Dedupe: storing the same content twice writes the same key twice, so the dictionary still holds one copy. Tamper-evidence: if someone edits a stored object, its contents no longer match its name, and you can check that.

blocks.title: hash_object
blocks.prompt: Write hash_object(store, kind, body). Build the bytes f"{kind} {len(body)}\0{body}", hash them with hashlib.sha1(...).hexdigest(), save store[oid] = (kind, body) and return oid. Storing the same body twice must leave one entry.
blocks.tests:
s = {}
a = hash_object(s, "blob", "hello\n")
assert a == "ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a", f"this is the id real git gives 'hello\\n'; got {a}"
assert s[a] == ("blob", "hello\n"), "the store should map the id to (kind, body)"
b = hash_object(s, "blob", "hello\n")
assert a == b and len(s) == 1, "same content must give the same id and be stored only once (dedupe)"
hash_object(s, "blob", "bye\n")
assert len(s) == 2, "different content gets a different id"
hints: Build the string with an f-string, then .encode() it before hashing: hashlib.sha1 wants bytes.
blocks.solution:
def hash_object(store, kind, body):
    data = f"{kind} {len(body)}\0{body}".encode()
    oid = hashlib.sha1(data).hexdigest()
    store[oid] = (kind, body)
    return oid

blocks.title: verify_store
blocks.prompt: find_tampered(store) should return the ids whose stored object no longer matches its name (someone edited the body after it was stored). It never finds anything. Fix it.
blocks.setup:
def oid_of(kind, body):
    return hashlib.sha1(f"{kind} {len(body)}\0{body}".encode()).hexdigest()
blocks.tests:
good = oid_of("blob", "rent: 900\n")
evil = oid_of("blob", "rent: 500\n")
store = {good: ("blob", "rent: 900\n"), evil: ("blob", "rent: 500\n")}
assert find_tampered(store) == [], "an untouched store has nothing tampered"
store[good] = ("blob", "rent: 9\n")
assert find_tampered(store) == [good], f"the edited object should be caught, got {find_tampered(store)}"
hints: What should the recomputed hash be compared with? The object's name is the hash it had when it was stored.

sections.title: Trees: a folder is a list of names

blocks.html: A blob has no filename. That's on purpose: two files with identical content (two copies of a licence, say) share one blob. The name lives one level up, in a tree: one line per file, name blob-id, sorted by name so the same folder always produces the same text, and so the same tree id.

blocks.title: write_tree turns {name: content} into a tree id
blocks.setup:
def hash_object(store, kind, body):
    oid = hashlib.sha1(f"{kind} {len(body)}\0{body}".encode()).hexdigest()
    store[oid] = (kind, body)
    return oid
blocks.tests:
s = {}
t1 = write_tree(s, {"b.txt": "two", "a.txt": "one"})
t2 = write_tree(s, {"a.txt": "one", "b.txt": "two"})
assert t1 == t2, "same folder in a different dict order must give the same tree id (sort the names)"
assert s[t1][0] == "tree" and s[t1][1].startswith("a.txt "), "the tree lists a.txt first"
assert len(s) == 3, "two blobs and one tree"

blocks.html: Now watch the sharing happen. Change one file and count which ids changed.
Two snapshots, three files each, but only 5 objects: the two unchanged blobs are shared. That's the "full snapshot that costs almost nothing" trick.

A commit is a tiny text object:

``` tree 3b18e5... parent 9f2c41...

add banana price ```

Because the commit's text includes its parent's id, its own id depends on the parent, which depends on its parent, all the way back. Change anything in old history and every later id changes. That's why you can't quietly rewrite a published commit.

A branch is not a copy of anything. It's a name pointing at one commit id: refs = {"main": "9f2c41..."}. Committing moves the pointer forward. HEAD says which branch you're on.

blocks.title: commit
blocks.prompt: Fill the blanks in commit. It writes the tree, builds the commit text with a parent line only when the branch already has a commit, saves it, and moves the branch pointer to the new commit.

def commit(store, refs, head, files, message):
    tree = write_tree(store, files)
    body = f"tree {tree}\n"

blocks.solution:
def commit(store, refs, head, files, message):
    tree = write_tree(store, files)
    body = f"tree {tree}\n"
    parent = refs.get(head)
    if parent:
        body += f"parent {parent}\n"
    body += f"\n{message}"
    oid = hash_object(store, "commit", body)
    refs[head] = oid
    return oid

blocks.html: Notice refs["idea"] = refs["main"]: creating a branch copies one id, not your files. That's why git branches are instant.

To show what changed between two commits, you don't compare file contents line by line first. Compare the trees: if a name has the same blob id on both sides, the file is identical and you skip it without reading it. Only names whose ids differ need a closer look.

blocks.title: diff_trees
blocks.prompt: Write diff_trees(old, new). Both are dicts {name: blob_id} (a tree already read back). Return a dict with three sorted lists: "added" (only in new), "removed" (only in old) and "changed" (in both, different id).
blocks.tests:
old = {"a.txt": "11", "b.txt": "22", "c.txt": "33"}
new = {"a.txt": "11", "b.txt": "99", "d.txt": "44"}
d = diff_trees(old, new)
assert d["added"] == ["d.txt"], f"d.txt is new, got {d['added']}"
assert d["removed"] == ["c.txt"], f"c.txt was removed, got {d['removed']}"
assert d["changed"] == ["b.txt"], f"only b.txt has a different blob id, got {d['changed']}"
assert diff_trees(old, old) == {"added": [], "removed": [], "changed": []}, "a tree compared with itself has no differences"
hints: Three comprehensions: names in new but not old, names in old but not new, and names in both whose ids differ.

blocks.html: In a real repo, trees contain other trees (sub-folders). If a sub-folder's tree id is the same on both sides, git skips the whole folder in one comparison. That's why git diff is fast even in huge projects.

Before you can merge main and idea, you need the commit where they split: the newest commit that both histories contain. It's called the merge base.

History is a graph where each commit points at its parents (a merge commit has two). The recipe:

  1. Collect every ancestor of a (including a) into a set.
  2. Walk back from b breadth-first (nearest commits first). The first commit you meet that is in the set is the merge base.

blocks.title: merge_base
blocks.prompt: Write merge_base(parents, a, b). parents maps each commit id to a list of parent ids (empty for the first commit). Return the closest common ancestor of a and b (a commit counts as its own ancestor). Return None if they share nothing.
blocks.tests:
#   A - B - C - D        (main)
#        \
#         E - F          (idea)
P = {"A": [], "B": ["A"], "C": ["B"], "D": ["C"], "E": ["B"], "F": ["E"]}
assert merge_base(P, "D", "F") == "B", f"main and idea split at B, got {merge_base(P, 'D', 'F')}"
assert merge_base(P, "F", "D") == "B", "the answer doesn't depend on the order"
assert merge_base(P, "D", "B") == "B", "if one is an ancestor of the other, it IS the merge base"
P2 = dict(P, G=["D", "F"], H=["F"])
assert merge_base(P2, "G", "H") == "F", "after merging idea into main (G), a newer idea commit H splits from G at F"
assert merge_base({"X": [], "Y": []}, "X", "Y") is None, "unrelated histories have no merge base"
hints: Part 1 is a plain graph walk with a stack and a seen set. Part 2 uses collections.deque so you look at the nearest commits first.
Remember a merge commit has two parents: always extend with the whole parents[c] list.

blocks.html:
Why do you need the base? Picture a.txt is different on your branch and on theirs. With only two versions you can't tell who changed it. With the base you can:

baseourstheirsresult
XXYY (only they changed it)
XYXY (only we changed it)
XYYY (we both made the same change)
XYZconflict: a human must decide

That's the whole idea of a three-way merge. A two-way comparison would call every difference a conflict.

blocks.code:
def pick(base, ours, theirs):
    if ours == theirs: return ours
    if ours == base: return theirs
    if theirs == base: return ours
    return "CONFLICT"

print(pick("x", "x", "y"))
print(pick("x", "y", "x"))
print(pick("x", "y", "y"))
print(pick("x", "y", "z"))
print(pick(None, None, "new file"))
